title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in San Francisco: Scale ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra carve two expanding frontiers—forward from start and backward from destination—then stitch them together. This is how modern route planning keeps shortest-path searches fast as graphs grow.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡—can you spot when the forward and backward waves meet?

In this SoMa street-grid visualization, Bidirectional Dijkstra runs two Dijkstra searches at once:
1) Forward search expands from the start node.
2) Backward search expands from the goal node (on the reversed graph).
3) The algorithm stops when the best possible path cannot be improved—then merges at the “meeting” frontier.

Why this matters for software engineering + route planning engines:
✅ Fewer explored nodes vs single-source Dijkstra
✅ Faster shortest path at scale (especially on large road graphs)
✅ Perfect for production where latency and throughput matter

Takeaway: Bidirectional search is a speed hack—two searches reduce the “search radius” until paths connect.

Debate question: Would you rather optimize for fewer node expansions (bidirectional) or simpler implementation (classic Dijkstra)?
